headline: Adrenaline
body: Directly, through the beta 2 receptor sitting on osteoblasts and chondrocytes.
punch: And deleting that receptor increases bone mass.

headline: Bone and cartilage
body: The same receptor class that responds to adrenaline and noradrenaline. Catecholamines act on these cells directly, not just by changing blood flow to them.
punch: Your sympathetic nervous system has a direct line into your skeleton.

headline: Knock the receptor out
body: Mice lacking beta 2 adrenergic receptors, either everywhere or only in osteoblasts, show increased bone mass. Removing a nervous system signal built more bone, which means the normal signal was restraining it.

headline: It also reaches
body: Catecholamines influence chondrocyte to osteoblast transdifferentiation. That's one of the four proposed routes by which growth plate cartilage converts into bone at closure.
punch: A stress signal sitting on top of a fate decision.

headline: Which is why
body: If beta 2 signalling restrains bone formation, blocking it should do the opposite. That prediction is why this receptor is studied in osteoporosis at all.
punch: The pharmacology follows directly from the knockout.

headline: The honest limit
body: Mouse genetics and cell level work. No human height outcome data exists for this pathway.
punch: Established in mice. Untested for height in people.

headline: What it does explain
body: Chronic stress raises catecholamine tone. That isn't a metaphor about cortisol, it's a specific receptor on your bone cells being activated more often.
punch: There's a physical receptor between stress and your skeleton.

headline: And why stimulants
body: Stimulant medication raises catecholamine signalling directly. That gives a concrete pathway linking it to the growth effects seen in paediatric data, separate from appetite.
punch: Two findings that looked unrelated share a receptor.
